docs.title: keyforge
docs.text:
Encryption and signing key lifecycle for Go applications: envelope encryption, automatic rotation without re-encrypting stored data, and controlled retirement and destruction.

Pre-release

keyforge has not been externally audited and is not yet recommended for production use. Read the threat model first.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Envelope encryption Data is encrypted with a data key; data keys are wrapped by a key-encryption key that a provider holds. Every ciphertext records which key version wrapped it. Rotation without re-encryption Rotating a key-encryption key re-wraps data keys. Stored data is not rewritten, and old versions stay readable until nothing references them. Controlled destruction Retiring or destroying a key is a separate, audited step that a caller-supplied guard can veto, so data under a legal hold is never made unrecoverable by accident. Crypto-shredding Per-subject keys make erasure a key destruction, tracked until every key version that wrapped the subject's keys is gone. Single host or shared A keyring file and a SQLite registry from one directory, or PostgreSQL for several replicas.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text:
• Not a secret store. Use a secret manager such as omnivault to hold secrets and to supply the local provider's root key.
  • Not a KMS. keyforge manages keys through providers; it does not replace a managed key service or a hardware module.
  • Not a cryptography library. It composes AES-256-GCM and HKDF-SHA-256 from the Go standard library and golang.org/x/crypto.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
sys, err := embedded.Open(ctx, embedded.Options{
    Dir:  "/var/lib/myapp/keyforge",
    Root: local.FileSource("/etc/keyforge/root.key"),
    Purposes: map[keyforge.Purpose]embedded.PurposeOptions{"session-secrets": {}},
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}
defer sys.Close()

sealed, err := sys.Client.Encrypt(ctx, "session-secrets", []byte("token-value"), []byte("user:42"))
plaintext, _, err := sys.Client.Decrypt(ctx, "session-secrets", sealed, []byte("user:42"))

Continue with Getting started.

docs.title: Envelope format
docs.text: This describes format version 1, the ciphertext keyforge writes. The format is frozen once data exists under it: a change needs a version bump, new known-answer vectors in envelope/testdata/vectors.json, and a fuzz run. Readers reject versions, modes, algorithms and flags they do not know, with typed errors, rather than guessing.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text: Mode Holds Use Reference (default) The data key's identifier; the wrapped key lives in the registry Rows and values under a purpose or subject. Rotating a key-encryption key re-wraps registry records, so stored data is never rewritten Inline The wrapped data key, the key-encryption key's identifier and the version, beside the ciphertext Standalone objects: exports, snapshots, files. A fresh data key per object

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Big-endian.

magic "KF" | format u8 | mode u8 | algorithm u8 | flags u8
purpose   : len u8 + bytes
reference : dek_id 16 bytes                          (reference mode)
inline    : kek_id 16 bytes, kek_version u32,
            wrapped_len u16, wrapped                 (inline mode)
nonce     : 12 bytes
ciphertext || tag
Field Rule format 1. Anything else is ErrUnsupportedFormat. mode 1 reference, 2 inline. Anything else is ErrUnknownMode. algorithm 1 is AES-256-GCM. Anything else is ErrUnknownAlgorithm. flags All eight bits are reserved and must be zero. A non-zero value is ErrUnsupportedFlags. purpose 1 to 255 bytes of lowercase ASCII letters, digits, ., _ and -, beginning with a letter or digit. reference A non-zero data key identifier and no inline fields. inline A non-zero key-encryption key identifier, a wrapped key of 1 to 65535 bytes, and no data key identifier.

An inconsistent header is ErrInvalidHeader, on write and on parse.

docs.title: What is authenticated
docs.text:
The AAD is the header bytes up to the nonce, followed by the caller's context. Changing the purpose, the key, the mode, the flags or the context makes decryption fail with ErrAuthentication. That error carries no detail: a wrong key, a changed header, a changed context and a modified ciphertext are not distinguished.

A data key is wrapped with its own AAD, which is also stored format:

Wrapped key AAD, in order Reference mode "keyforge/dek/v1\0", purpose, subject, data key identifier, key-encryption key identifier Inline mode "keyforge/inline/v1\0", purpose, key-encryption key identifier

The purpose and the subject are each length-prefixed with a big-endian u32. A wrapped key therefore cannot be moved to another purpose or subject, or presented under another identity.

docs.title: Text form
docs.text: kf1. followed by unpadded base64url of the binary form, for text columns and JSON. There is one spelling: padding, line breaks, the standard alphabet and non-canonical trailing bits are rejected with ErrBadTextForm. A well-formed prefix for another version is ErrUnsupportedFormat.

docs.title: Algorithm 1: AES-256-GCM
docs.text:
AES-256-GCM through cipher.NewGCMWithRandomNonce, the only GCM constructor permitted under GODEBUG=fips140=only. The AEAD generates its own random nonce; the format stores it in the header's nonce field and restores it on open. An AEAD that takes an explicit nonce is refused (ErrNotRandomNonce), so a nonce can never be chosen by a caller.

Random 96-bit nonces limit one key to far fewer than 2³² encryptions. keyforge counts encryptions per data key, in blocks reserved from the registry, and moves to a new data key epoch at the cap (default 2³⁰) or at the maximum age (default 90 days), whichever comes first. The cap holds across replicas and crashes: an unused part of a reserved block counts as used, so the count can overstate and never understate.

docs.title: Typed errors
docs.text: ErrBadMagic, ErrTruncated, ErrUnsupportedFormat, ErrUnknownMode, ErrUnknownAlgorithm, ErrUnsupportedFlags, ErrInvalidPurpose, ErrInvalidHeader, ErrBadTextForm and ErrAuthentication. Those that report a value carry it in a ValueError.

docs.title: The keyring file
docs.text:
The local provider's keyring has its own format, also frozen once a keyring exists: a fixed 32-byte header, authenticated as additional data, then the sealed payload.

magic "KFKR" | format u8 | reserved u8 | algorithm u8 | reserved u8
root key ID : 16 bytes
generation  : u64, big-endian
sealed      : nonce (12) || ciphertext || tag

The payload is sealed with AES-256-GCM under a key derived from the root key with HKDF-SHA-256. The root-key identifier is derived from the same root key under a different context, so it identifies the key without revealing it. The generation increases with every change and can be read without the root key, which is how a restored older copy is detected. Reserved bytes must be zero, and anything unrecognized is ErrCorruptKeyring.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This guide takes a single host from nothing to encrypted data with rotation running. It uses the embedded package, which wires a keyring file, a SQLite registry, the lifecycle jobs and the control plane from a directory and a root key. Larger deployments assemble the same pieces themselves; the technical requirements describe each.

docs.title: The root key
docs.text:
The keyring file holds your key-encryption keys, sealed under a root key. The root key is 32 random bytes, and it is the one secret keyforge cannot recover for you. Generate it once and keep it somewhere other than the state directory:

keyforge rootkey generate > /etc/keyforge/root.key
chmod 600 /etc/keyforge/root.key

Put a copy in a secret manager or an offline store as well. See operations for what to do and why.

A root key file in the keyring's directory is refused, and so is one readable by group or others.

docs.title: Open the system
docs.text:
sys, err := embedded.Open(ctx, embedded.Options{
    Dir:  "/var/lib/myapp/keyforge",
    Root: local.FileSource("/etc/keyforge/root.key"),
    Purposes: map[keyforge.Purpose]embedded.PurposeOptions{
        "session-secrets": {},
        "customer-notes":  {PerSubject: true},
    },
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}
defer sys.Close()

On the first start this creates the directory, the keyring and the registry, and a key-encryption key with its first version active for each purpose. On every later start it changes nothing. A purpose is a name for what the data is for; it is part of what a ciphertext is bound to, so a value encrypted for one purpose cannot be opened as another.

Purpose names are 1 to 255 bytes of lowercase letters, digits, ., _ and -, beginning with a letter or digit.

PerSubject: true gives each subject (a user, a tenant) data keys of its own, which is what makes erasing one subject possible. See operations.

docs.title: Encrypt and decrypt
docs.text:
sealed, err := sys.Client.Encrypt(ctx, "session-secrets", []byte("token-value"), []byte("user:42"))
if err != nil {
    return err
}
text := sealed.String() // "kf1." and base64url: safe for a text column or JSON

plaintext, info, err := sys.Client.Decrypt(ctx, "session-secrets", sealed, []byte("user:42"))

The last argument is a context: bytes that are authenticated but not stored, such as the row's key. Decryption fails unless the same bytes are supplied, so a ciphertext copied to another row does not open there. Use something your application can always reconstruct.

For a per-subject purpose, write with EncryptFor:

sealed, err := sys.Client.EncryptFor(ctx, "customer-notes", "customer-17", note, []byte("note:9"))

Decrypt needs no subject: the envelope names its data key and the registry knows whose it is. Parse a stored envelope with envelope.ParseText.

Decrypt reports whether the envelope is stale (written under a data key that is no longer current). Rewriting stale values as you meet them is optional; nothing breaks if you never do, because rotation does not depend on it.

For a standalone object such as a file or an export, EncryptInline carries the wrapped key with the ciphertext instead of recording it in the registry. Inline objects are not found by a re-wrap; see operations.

docs.title: Run the lifecycle jobs
docs.text:
go func() {
    if err := sys.Run(ctx); err != nil {
        log.Print(err)
    }
}()

Run rotates keys when they are due, moves data keys off old versions, and completes retirements and erasures that are ready. It resumes any work a previous process left unfinished. Defaults: a key-encryption key rotates every 365 days, a data key epoch ends after 90 days or 2³⁰ encryptions, and a rotated version is kept for at least 30 days before it can be retired. Set Policy in the options to change them per purpose.

Nothing is retired or destroyed unless you supply a Guard, because the absence of a veto is not consent. Rotation and re-wrapping, which lose nothing, run without one.

docs.title: Expose the control plane
docs.text:
The HTTP control plane exists only when you supply an authorizer, and it asks before every action:

opts.Authorizer = service.AuthorizerFunc(func(ctx context.Context, a service.Action, purpose string) error {
    // Return nil to allow, service.ErrUnauthenticated if there is no identity,
    // or any other error to forbid. The identity is whatever your middleware
    // put on ctx.
    return checkAdmin(ctx, a, purpose)
})

h, err := sys.Handler()
if err != nil {
    return err
}
go http.ListenAndServe("127.0.0.1:8480", h)

There is no default allow. Actions include status.read, keys.rotate, keys.retire.request, keys.destroy and shred.request; give each caller only the ones it needs.

Then use the command line:

export KEYFORGE_SERVER=http://127.0.0.1:8480
keyforge status
keyforge verify

keyforge status shows every key, what is overdue, backups and provider health. keyforge health exits non-zero and lists the problems, for a monitor. keyforge verify round-trips a test value through each purpose's keys from a cold start, which is the quickest way to learn that a key is usable.

docs.title: Back it up
docs.text: A backup is the keyring and the registry together, taken at the same time, plus the root key kept apart. Read operations before relying on a deployment: a backup you have not restored from is a hope.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text: What to watch, what to do on a schedule, and what to do when something goes wrong. Commands assume KEYFORGE_SERVER points at the control plane; see getting started.

docs.title: What runs by itself
docs.text:
With the lifecycle jobs running, keyforge:

  • Rotates a key-encryption key when its interval has passed (default 365 days) and records a sentinel for the new version.
  • Re-wraps the data keys under older versions to the active one, in batches, resuming after a crash. Stored data is never rewritten.
  • Advances a data key to a new epoch at its encryption cap or maximum age (default 2³⁰ encryptions or 90 days), as writes happen.
  • Requests retirement of versions outside the retained floor, which starts their delay, and completes it and destroys the material once the delay has passed and nothing references the version, each only where the guard allows.
  • Completes erasures whose key versions have all been destroyed.

With no guard configured, nothing is retired or destroyed: the absence of a veto is not consent. A version whose retirement was requested waits, and the guard is asked again on each pass. Emergency procedures are never started by the jobs; a person starts them.

Policy is set per purpose through embedded.Options.Policy:

Setting Default Meaning KEKInterval 365 days How long a version is active DEKMaxAge 90 days How long a data key epoch takes writes DEKMaxEncryptions 2³⁰ Encryptions per data key RetirementDelay 30 days Wait between asking to retire a version and doing it RetainVersions 2 Versions never retired: the active one and the newest decrypt-only. At least 2, so the previous version remains as the rollback margin RequireBackup off Rotation waits for the keyring backup to be acknowledged

The retirement delay must be at least ten times the client cache TTL, so that a process holding a cached view cannot keep wrapping under a version already eligible for retirement.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
keyforge status is the full picture: each purpose, its key versions and states, what is overdue, backup state, provider health, jobs that failed and erasures pending. keyforge health exits non-zero and lists the problems in words, so a monitor can alert on it. keyforge status --json is for tooling.

Attention is needed when status reports:

Report Meaning Do A rotation overdue The job did not run or keeps failing Check the jobs section for the failure; fix the cause; or keyforge rotate <purpose> Keyring ahead of its backup A change is not in the backup you last acknowledged Back up and acknowledge (below) A provider unhealthy The keyring cannot be read or unlocked Check the file, its mode and the root key source A purpose with no usable key Nothing can be written Fix the provider; do not work around it A job failed repeatedly Backoff is lengthening Read the failure; it names the step

keyforge verify round-trips a test value through each purpose's keys from a cold start. Run it after a deploy, a restore or a change to the root key source. It checks that keys are usable, which status cannot.

docs.title: The root key
docs.text:
The root key seals the keyring. Everything else can be rebuilt from a keyring and a registry; the root key cannot be rebuilt from anything. Lose it and every key-encryption key in the keyring is gone, and with them everything wrapped under them.

  • Generate 32 random bytes: keyforge rootkey generate. keyforge does not stretch a passphrase, because a passphrase is not a key.
  • Keep it out of the state directory and out of the keyring's backup. A backup that holds both the keyring and the root key is the keyring in the clear.
  • Hold two copies: one in the secret manager the process reads it from, one offline (a sealed envelope in a safe, a hardware token, a second person's password manager). keyforge does not split or escrow it for you, because that would mean implementing a secret-sharing scheme; use one you already trust.
  • Test the second copy. Restore into a scratch directory using only the offline copy and run keyforge verify against it. An escrow you have not read back is not one.
  • Rotate it when someone who held it leaves or a copy may have been seen: Keyring.RotateRootKey(ctx, next) re-encrypts the keyring under the new root key in one atomic write. Update the source the process reads from, and both stored copies, before the next restart. This protects the keyring file from now on. It does not rotate any key-encryption key: a keyring copy taken earlier, together with the old root key, still yields live keys, so after a suspected exposure of the root key also rotate the key-encryption keys and retire the old versions.

A wrong root key is refused with ErrWrongRootKey before anything is decrypted, so a mistake is reported as what it is and not as a corrupt file.

docs.title: Backup and restore
docs.text:
A backup has three parts, and they belong together:

  1. The keyring file (keyring.kf).
  2. The registry: it holds the wrapped data keys and the state of every key version. Without it the keyring cannot say which data keys it protects.
  3. The root key, kept apart from both (see above).

docs.title: Taking a backup
docs.text:
keyforge keyring inspect /var/lib/myapp/keyforge/keyring.kf
# generation: 14   root key ID: 5f1c…

Copy the keyring file. Copy the registry with System.BackupRegistry(ctx, path), which writes a consistent snapshot of the SQLite registry while the system is running (copying the database file on its own is not a backup, because recent writes sit in the write-ahead log). For PostgreSQL use its own tooling. Then tell keyforge which keyring generation the copy holds:

keyforge backup ack local --generation 14 --note "offsite bucket, daily"

With RequireBackup set, a rotation waits until the acknowledgement catches up. What it guarantees is narrow: a rotation does not start while the previous keyring generation is unbacked, so unbacked rotations cannot pile up. It does not protect the new version itself. A disk lost right after a rotation loses what was wrapped under the new version, whatever the setting, so take and acknowledge a copy straight after every rotation.

docs.title: Restoring
docs.text:
Stop the process first, then restore the keyring and the registry from the same backup, and open with AcceptRollback: true. A keyring file replaced under a running process is refused at the next write, but the process keeps its in-memory copy until it restarts. Without it, a keyring older than one this host has seen is refused with ErrKeyringRolledBack, naming both generations, so that a stale copy is never used by mistake.

The highest generation this host has seen is kept beside the keyring in keyring.kf.backup, authenticated under a key derived from the root key, so it cannot be edited or forged without the root key. Removing it does not switch the check off: a keyring past generation 1 with no such file is refused with ErrBackupStateMissing, and one that does not authenticate with ErrCorruptBackupState. Moving a keyring to a new host without that file, or replacing a damaged one, therefore also needs AcceptRollback: true once. The check cannot tell an older keyring restored together with its own older state file from the real thing; keep the keys directory writable only by the service.

Upgrading from a version that did not authenticate the state file. The first open after the upgrade fails with ErrUnauthenticatedBackupState. Confirm the keyring on disk is the one you expect (keyforge keyring inspect), then open once with AcceptRollback: true; the existing high-water mark and backup acknowledgement are kept and the file is rewritten authenticated.

What a restore loses. The registry holds data keys. Any data key created after the registry backup is not in it, and data encrypted under such a key cannot be decrypted. Back up the registry as often as you can afford to lose data written between backups; on PostgreSQL, point-in-time recovery closes the gap. A keyring copy is cheap and changes only on rotation, so acknowledge a fresh one after every rotation.

A restore can undo an erasure. Shredded subjects, their tombstones and the destroyed state of their data keys live in the registry, so restoring a registry backup taken before a shred brings the subject's keys back and removes the tombstone. Keep a record of requested erasures outside the registry, and repeat them after any restore. keyforge does not replay them.

After a restore, run keyforge verify, then keyforge status.

A missing keyring beside a registry that holds keys is refused with ErrKeyringMissing rather than recreated, because an empty keyring would make every operation fail beside a registry that looks healthy.

docs.title: Manual rotation
docs.text:
keyforge rotate <purpose>      # activate the next version
keyforge rewrap <purpose>      # move data keys off every non-active version
keyforge rollback <purpose>    # reactivate the most recent decrypt-only version

Rolling back is for a version that turns out to be bad (a provider fault, a configuration error): nothing needs recovering, because the earlier version was kept. Data keys already wrapped under the demoted version still unwrap under it.

docs.title: Retiring and destroying a version
docs.text:
Retirement and destruction are separate steps, each asking the guard:

keyforge retire request <kek> <version>    # starts the delay
keyforge retire complete <kek> <version>   # after the delay, if no data key is under it and the guard allows
keyforge retire cancel   <kek> <version>   # back to decrypt-only
keyforge destroy <kek> <version>           # destroy the material, if the guard allows

A retired version is not usable even before its material is destroyed, so retiring has an effect on its own, and data wrapped under it outside the registry becomes unreadable at retirement, not at destruction. Destruction is irreversible: after it, only a backup that holds the keyring can bring the version back.

The guard is yours to write. It sees the action, the purpose, the version, how many registry data keys still reference it, and who asked, and returns allow, deny or pending. It exists to know what keyforge cannot: that an export, a snapshot or a backup somewhere still needs the version, or that data is under a legal hold. A deny at retirement returns the version to service with the denial recorded. A deny at destruction leaves the version retired: it can no longer be used, and only destruction remains for it, so the guard's useful veto is the one at retirement. A guard that fails, or is absent, advances nothing.

docs.title: Data outside the registry
docs.text: Inline envelopes carry their wrapped key with them, so the registry does not know they exist and a re-wrap does not move them. Retiring a version while an inline object is still wrapped under it makes the object unreadable once the material is destroyed. Before retiring a version, find and re-encrypt inline objects (Reencrypt brings an envelope up to the current key) or confirm they are gone. The guard is where that check belongs.

docs.title: Emergencies
docs.text: Emergency procedures differ from scheduled work in three ways: they do not wait for a backup acknowledgement, they have no retirement delay, and the guard is asked and its answer recorded, but it cannot block them. Exposure is not a time to wait for an approval.

docs.title: A key-encryption key version is exposed
docs.text:
keyforge compromise <kek> <version>

This replaces the version if it is active (the demotion and the new activation are one transaction, so there is never a moment with no active version), marks it compromised, re-wraps every data key away from it, asks the guard and records the answer, then retires and destroys it. It is idempotent and resumable: if some data key cannot be moved, the version stays compromised and referenced, is not destroyed, and the call reports what remains. Call it again.

--keep-material stops after retirement, leaving the material at the provider so you can recover inline objects before destroying it through the usual path.

Re-wrapping protects data keys going forward. It cannot un-expose a key that was read: data encrypted under a data key the attacker could unwrap must be treated as exposed. For that, the data key's own procedure applies.

docs.title: A data key is exposed
docs.text:
keyforge datakey compromise <id>   # replaces it and marks it compromised

The key stays readable so that what it protects can be re-encrypted. The host does that, as it meets each record or in a pass of its own, with Reencrypt; keyforge cannot, because the data is the application's. The report gives an upper bound on how much was encrypted under the key. When the host is done:

keyforge datakey destroy <id>

docs.title: Erasing a subject
docs.text:
For a per-subject purpose:

keyforge shred request <purpose> <subject>
keyforge shred status  <purpose> <subject>

Requesting destroys the subject's data keys at once, so its data is unrecoverable from the live system wherever the ciphertext was copied. A new key for the subject is then refused: an erasure that quietly re-enrolled the subject would not be one.

The erasure is not complete until every key-encryption key version that ever wrapped one of the subject's keys is destroyed, because a registry backup taken earlier still holds them wrapped under one of those versions. "Complete" speaks for the live system only: a keyring backup taken before the versions were destroyed still holds their material, and together with a registry backup from before the shred it recovers the subject. Expire keyring and registry backups from before an erasure on the same schedule as the erasure. shred status lists the versions outstanding and an expected date. With the defaults that is more than two years for a version that is active today, plus your backup retention. A purpose that needs faster erasure sets a shorter KEKInterval.

A client that has the subject's key cached keeps using it until the entry expires or Client.Purge is called; purge the clients if the erasure must be effective immediately. That covers writes as well as reads: a process holding the key goes on writing under it, and nothing it writes can be read by another process or after a restart. Shredding a purpose that is not per-subject erases nothing, and a purpose with no key is refused.

docs.title: Limits to plan around
docs.text:
• The local provider is as safe as the host and its root key source. It is not a hardware module, and it is the wrong choice where managed keys are required.
  • The durable job state is for one process. Several replicas sharing a registry need a shared job provider; the keyforge scheduler works with any OmniWorkflow provider.
  • Inline-mode objects each wrap a fresh data key under the active key-encryption key version with a random nonce, and there is no count of wraps per version. Keep a version's inline writes well under 2³² by rotating on a schedule that fits your volume.
  • Another process that destroys a key version does not take effect in a running provider that has already loaded its material until that provider reloads; destruction is not instant across processes.
  • keyforge depends on the host clock for scheduling. A clock set far ahead makes rotations and retirement delays come due early.
  • Go cannot lock or reliably zero memory: cached keys can appear in a memory dump or swap.

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text:
What keyforge defends, against whom, and where it stops. The design is in the technical requirements; this is the part a reviewer reads first.

keyforge has not been externally audited. It composes standard primitives from the Go standard library and golang.org/x/crypto and implements none of its own; the risk it adds is in how they are combined and in key lifecycle.

docs.title: Assets and attackers
docs.text:
The assets are key-encryption key material, data key material, the plaintext the data keys protect, and the ability to destroy keys.

Attacker Has What keyforge offers Reads the database The registry: wrapped data keys, key states The registry holds wrapped keys and never a plaintext one. It yields no key and cannot move a ciphertext to another record. Reads a backup The keyring and the registry The keyring is sealed under the root key, which is held apart. A backup without the root key is ciphertext. Reads the ciphertext store Envelopes AEAD authentication; the AAD binds purpose, mode, key identity and caller context. Modifies stored data Write access to rows Tampering fails authentication. Moving an envelope to another record fails if the caller binds a context. Reaches the control plane Network access The authorizer is asked before every action and there is no default allow. Compromises the host process Code execution as the application Not defended. See below.

docs.title: Mitigations
docs.text: Asset Threat Mitigation Key-encryption key material Read from disk or backup Sealed under a root key held apart from the keyring; keyring mode 0600, group- or other-readable refused; a root key file beside the keyring refused Key-encryption key material Wrong or stale keyring used A wrong root key is refused before decryption; a keyring older than one seen is refused unless the restore is accepted; the high-water mark is authenticated under the root key and a missing one is refused past generation 1 Data key material Memory read Bounded cache with a TTL; best-effort zeroing Ciphertext Moved between purposes, subjects or records AAD binds the purpose and the caller's context; the wrapped key is bound to its purpose, subject and identity Ciphertext Tampering AES-256-GCM authentication Nonce reuse Random-nonce collision One counted cap per data key, enforced across replicas and crashes in blocks; epochs advance before the limit Availability Provider or registry outage A cache; beyond it, operations fail closed and say so; reads are unaffected by a write-side outage Data under retention Premature destruction A separate guard consulted at retirement and again at destruction; a delay; every outcome audited Rotation A restored stale backup loses data Keyring generation and backup acknowledgement; rotation can wait on it Erasure A backup restores a shredded key A shred is complete only when every key version that ever wrapped the subject's keys is destroyed in the live keyring. Backups are the operator's: see the limitations Control plane Unauthorized rotation or destruction Host-supplied authorizer on every action; audit of administrative reads Logs Key material in an error or event Key material never leaves its owner: it is not logged, not in errors and not in audit events

docs.title: Fail closed
docs.text: With no usable key, an operation fails; it never falls back to a weaker path. There is no network call per encrypt or decrypt: the data path is in process. An algorithm outside the active profile is refused, and the profile can narrow the set and never widen it. The code stays valid under GODEBUG=fips140=only.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• The local provider is as safe as the host and its root key source. It is not a hardware module and is unsuitable where managed keys are required.
  • Memory. Go cannot lock or reliably zero memory. Cached keys can appear in memory dumps and swap.
  • A compromised process can use the keys it can use. keyforge limits the blast radius by purpose and subject; it does not defeat an attacker who controls the process.
  • The root key is not recoverable. Its loss is the loss of the keyring. keyforge does not escrow it.
  • Backups of the registry lose recent data keys. Data written under a data key created after the last registry backup is unreadable after a restore.
  • Scheduling depends on the host clock.
  • Inline objects are invisible to the registry. Retiring a version relies on the host's statement that nothing outside the registry needs it.
  • A restore can undo an erasure. Shreds and tombstones live in the registry; restoring an older registry resurrects the subject's keys, and a keyring backup holds destroyed versions' material. Erasure is complete for the live system only.
  • A matched restore of keyring and state file is not detected. The high-water mark lives beside the keyring. Someone who can write the keys directory and holds an older copy of both the keyring and its state file can put them back together; detecting that needs state kept somewhere they cannot write.
  • A restore under a running process. An older keyring copy put in place while the process runs is refused at the next write and at the next open, but the process keeps using its in-memory copy until restarted. Stop the process before restoring.
  • Unauthenticated envelopes cost work. A parsed inline envelope with an unseen key reference makes a registry call and a provider unwrap, and bogus versions can evict cache entries. This cannot disclose a key.
  • Inline wraps are not counted against the key-encryption key version they are wrapped under.
  • Erasure takes as long as key retirement. A shred is complete only when the key versions that wrapped the subject's keys are destroyed; until then a restored registry backup can recover the data.
  • Cached keys outlive a shred or a retirement for up to the cache TTL, or until Purge.
  • Not externally audited.

docs.title: v0.1.0
docs.text: Release Date: 2026-10-12

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Envelope encryption with rotation that does not touch your data. Data keys are wrapped by provider-held key-encryption keys, so rotating a key-encryption key re-wraps registry records and leaves stored ciphertext alone.
  • Guarded retirement and destruction. A caller-supplied guard can veto, a delay applies, every outcome is audited, and the absence of a guard is a refusal.
  • Erasure by key destruction. Per-subject keys make erasing a subject a key destruction, with completion tracked until every key version that wrapped the subject's keys is gone.
  • A single-host setup in one call. embedded.Open wires a keyring file, a SQLite registry, the lifecycle jobs and the control plane from a directory and a root key. PostgreSQL is supported for shared deployments.

docs.text: keyforge v0.1.0 has not been externally audited and is not yet recommended for production use. The envelope format and the keyring file format are frozen from this release: a change needs a version bump and new known-answer vectors. See the threat model for what it defends and where it stops.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: keyforge manages the lifecycle of encryption keys for Go applications. It composes standard primitives from the Go standard library and golang.org/x/crypto, implements none of its own, and keeps the code that touches key material to the standard library alone, which a test enforces.

docs.title: Envelope format
docs.text:
Mode Holds Use Reference The data key's identifier; the wrapped key is in the registry Rows and values under a purpose or subject Inline The wrapped key beside the ciphertext Standalone objects such as exports and files

AES-256-GCM through cipher.NewGCMWithRandomNonce, with the header and the caller's context authenticated. A per-key encryption cap holds across replicas and crashes, and data keys move to a new epoch by volume and by age. See Envelope format.

docs.title: Rotation and recovery
docs.text:
• Automatic KEK rotation with a sentinel recorded for every version
  • Resumable, idempotent re-wrapping of data keys, safe to run from several workers
  • Rollback to the most recent decrypt-only version
  • Emergency procedures for an exposed key-encryption key or data key
  • Keyring backup acknowledgement and rollback detection

docs.title: Retirement, destruction and erasure
docs.text:
• Retirement in steps: request, delay, guard, complete; then destruction behind the guard again
  • Crypto-shredding of a subject with a tombstone, tracked to completion

docs.title: Providers and stores
docs.text:
Component Included Provider Keyring file sealed under a root key; in-memory provider for tests Registry SQLite and PostgreSQL through Ent; in-memory reference store Scheduler OmniWorkflow: in-memory, durable file store, Temporal, Step Functions

Every provider and every store passes a shared conformance suite.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
• HTTP control plane; an authorizer is asked before every action and there is no default allow
  • keyforge command line: status, health, verify, rotate, rewrap, rollback, retire, destroy, compromise, datakey, shred, backup ack, keyring inspect, rootkey generate
  • Status report, audit events and a metrics interface with bounded labels

docs.text:

go install github.com/plexusone/keyforge/cmd/keyforge@v0.1.0

Requires Go 1.26.

docs.text:
sys, err := embedded.Open(ctx, embedded.Options{
    Dir:  "/var/lib/myapp/keyforge",
    Root: local.FileSource("/etc/keyforge/root.key"),
    Purposes: map[keyforge.Purpose]embedded.PurposeOptions{"session-secrets": {}},
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}
defer sys.Close()

sealed, err := sys.Client.Encrypt(ctx, "session-secrets", []byte("token-value"), []byte("user:42"))
plaintext, _, err := sys.Client.Decrypt(ctx, "session-secrets", sealed, []byte("user:42"))

See Getting started and Operations.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• The local provider is as safe as the host and its root key source. It is not a hardware module.
  • The root key is not recoverable. Keep two copies, one offline.
  • A restore can undo an erasure. Shreds live in the registry, and keyring backups hold destroyed versions' material. Erasure is complete for the live system only.
  • Restores are done with the process stopped. A keyring replaced under a running process is refused at the next write, but the process keeps its in-memory copy.
  • Writes under a cached key outlive a shred until the cache expires or Purge is called.
  • Inline wraps are not counted per key-encryption key version.
  • Registry backups lose recent data keys. Data written under a key created after the last backup is unreadable after a restore.
  • One process for durable jobs. Several replicas need a shared OmniWorkflow provider.

The complete list is in the threat model.

docs.title: v0.2.0
docs.text: Release Date: 2026-10-25

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• The rollback check can no longer be switched off from the keys directory. The highest keyring generation a host has seen is now authenticated under the root key, so an older keyring cannot be put back by editing or deleting the state file beside it.
  • A rollback margin is always kept. A policy must retain at least the active key version and the previous one.
  • Two breaking changes. The first open after upgrading needs AcceptRollback once, and RetainVersions below 2 is rejected. See Upgrading.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: keyforge v0.2.0 has not been externally audited and is not yet recommended for production use. The envelope format and the keyring file format are unchanged from v0.1.0. See the threat model for what it defends and where it stops.

docs.title: Authenticated rollback high-water mark
docs.text:
The local provider keeps the highest keyring generation it has seen in a state file beside the keyring (<keyring>.backup, keyring.kf.backup under embedded). Before this release that file was plain JSON, and a missing file was read as "nothing seen". Anyone able to write the keys directory could put back an older, still validly sealed keyring and delete or edit the state file, and Open accepted the older keyring without AcceptRollback, bringing back key versions that had been destroyed or undoing a rotation.

The state file is now authenticated with HMAC-SHA-256 under a key derived from the root key with HKDF, and bound to the keyring's file name. Open refuses:

Condition Error A state file that does not authenticate local.ErrCorruptBackupState No state file beside a keyring past generation 1 local.ErrBackupStateMissing A state file in the previous, unauthenticated format local.ErrUnauthenticatedBackupState

Generation 1 without a state file is still accepted, since a crash during Create leaves exactly that. Each refusal can be accepted with AcceptRollback, which rewrites the state authenticated and keeps any existing high-water mark and backup acknowledgement. Root key rotation authenticates the state under both the old and the new root key before replacing the keyring, so a crash on either side leaves state that the surviving keyring's root key opens.

The check still cannot tell an older keyring restored together with its own older state file from the real thing; keep the keys directory writable only by the service.

docs.title: Retained-versions floor of 2
docs.text: Policy validation accepted RetainVersions: 1, which let a deployment retire the previous key version as soon as a rotation completed and lose the rollback margin. Policy.Validate and Set.Validate, and so rotate.New, now reject a value below 2 in the default and in every per-purpose override. The active version and the previous one are always kept, and only N-2 and older can be retired. A compromised version is still not counted by the floor and can be retired and destroyed at once.

docs.title: 1. Open each existing keyring once with AcceptRollback
docs.text:
The first Open of a keyring written by v0.1.0 fails with ErrUnauthenticatedBackupState. For each keyring:

  1. Stop the process.

  2. Confirm the keyring on disk is the one you expect:

    keyforge keyring inspect

  3. Open it once with AcceptRollback: true:

    sys, err := embedded.Open(ctx, embedded.Options{
    Dir:            "/var/lib/myapp/keyforge",
    Root:           local.FileSource("/etc/keyforge/root.key"),
    AcceptRollback: true, // once, for the upgrade
    Purposes:       purposes,
})

    With the local provider directly, set AcceptRollback: true in local.Options.

  4. Remove AcceptRollback again and restart. Leaving it set accepts a rolled back keyring on every open.

The existing high-water mark and backup acknowledgement are kept; the state file is rewritten in the authenticated format.

The same one-time step is needed when a keyring past generation 1 is opened without its state file, for example after moving it to a new host (ErrBackupStateMissing).

docs.title: 2. Keep at least two versions
docs.text:
If any policy sets RetainVersions to 1, rotate.New and policy validation now return an error. Set it to 2 or more, or leave it zero to inherit the default of 2, in the default policy and in every per-purpose override:

policy.Policy{
    RetainVersions: 2, // or 0 to inherit the default
}

A deployment that relied on retiring the previous version straight after a rotation now retires it one rotation later.

docs.text:
go get github.com/plexusone/keyforge@v0.2.0
go install github.com/plexusone/keyforge/cmd/keyforge@v0.2.0

Requires Go 1.26.

docs.title: keyforge: Plan
docs.text:
Initiative: INIT-KEYFORGE-001 Repository: github.com/plexusone/keyforge

Implements the PRD and TRD. The roadmap holds the work items and their status.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
• Format first. The envelope format is the one thing that cannot change after data exists, so it is specified, vectored and fuzzed before any provider or scheduler is built on it.
  • Library before control plane. The data path (encrypt, decrypt, cache) is complete and tested with the in-memory store and the local provider before the scheduler, service and CLI exist.
  • Conformance suites with the interfaces. The provider and store conformance suites are written with the interfaces, so each later implementation inherits them.
  • Public-ready from the first commit. Specs, history and docs carry no internal facts; the security policy and threat model exist before the first release.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text: Phase Theme Outcome 1 Envelope and core library A tested format and Client over an in-memory registry and a test provider 2 Local provider and registry A real keyring provider with safe writes, and the store interface with an in-memory implementation and conformance suite 3 Rotation, policy and retirement Automatic KEK and DEK rotation with rollback, resumable jobs, the guard, the delay, and per-subject shredding 4 Control plane Scheduler with leader lease, audit sink, status, the service and the CLI 5 Hardening and v0.1.0 SQL store, crash and property tests, documentation, security review, release 6 Rotation and disaster-recovery drills Weekly canary rotation, the unattended DR drill and its analyst-written report; v0.2.0 7 Inventory and crypto specification External boundary inventory and export of the system's crypto specification for verification

docs.title: Dependencies and sequencing
docs.text:
• Phase 2's provider conformance suite depends on the Provider interface fixed in phase 1.
  • Phase 3 depends on the registry state machine from phase 2.
  • Phase 4's scheduler depends on phase 3's jobs; the SQL store in phase 5 depends on the store conformance suite from phase 2.
  • Phase 6's drills depend on the scheduler and status from phase 4. They follow v0.1.0 rather than gate it: a KEK rotates yearly by default, so no deployment reaches its first real rotation before the canary ships.
  • systemforge integration (guard, audit sink, catalog granularity, and a Sampler implementation that reads sample envelopes from the encrypted columns of registered entities) follows v0.1.0 and is tracked in systemforge. The Sampler interface is defined in keyforge, which calls it, and is optional, so the drill runs before the integration exists.

docs.text: Risk Mitigation Format mistakes found after release Vectors and fuzzing before phase 2; a format version byte and typed errors for unknown values Keyring corruption or loss Atomic writes, generation counter, backup acknowledgement, crash tests Rotation job leaves a mixed state Idempotent batches with a cursor; both versions stay readable throughout Scope creep into a KMS or secret store The non-goals in the PRD; providers and omnivault cover those Perceived rolling of own crypto Standard primitives only; the format reviewed before release

docs.text: v0.1.0 when phase 5 completes and CI is green on all platforms. The release notes state the maturity (pre-1.0, not externally audited), the threat model and the known limitations. v0.2.0 adds the rotation and DR drills when phase 6 completes.

docs.title: keyforge: Product Requirements
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-KEYFORGE-001 Repository: github.com/plexusone/keyforge

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Applications that encrypt data end up with a private, ad hoc key mechanism per feature: a key in an environment variable for sessions, another for backups, a signing key on disk. Each has the same gaps:

  • Rotation is a project. Changing a key means re-encrypting everything it protects, so keys are never rotated, or are rotated rarely and with downtime.
  • No record of which key protects what. When a key is suspected compromised there is no inventory of the data it covers.
  • No safe way to destroy. Privacy erasure has to reach backups and replicas, and retention duties (legal hold) can forbid destroying a key at all. Nothing in the key mechanism knows either.
  • Single-host and cloud deployments differ. A solo developer starts with a file; a production system uses a managed key service. Moving between them should not rewrite stored data.

Managed cloud services solve rotation well (a key keeps its identifier, gains new key material, and old material stays available for decryption), but applications still have to model purposes, per-subject keys, destruction policy and audit around them, and cannot rely on a managed service when running locally.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. One interface for all application encryption, independent of where the root keys live.
  2. Rotation without re-encrypting stored data and without downtime, done automatically on a schedule.
  3. A versioned, self-describing ciphertext format, so any record can be decrypted, rotated or destroyed knowing only what is stored beside it.
  4. Destruction as a controlled, audited operation that a caller can veto, including crypto-shredding of per-subject data.
  5. Works from a single file key to a managed KMS by configuration.
  6. Reviewable. Small surface, standard primitives, public, with a stated threat model.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Implementing cryptographic primitives. keyforge composes the Go standard library and golang.org/x/crypto.
  • Replacing a KMS or HSM. Root keys stay in the provider.
  • Storing application secrets, passwords or API keys. That is a secret manager's job.
  • TLS certificate lifecycle in v1. Certificates and other key types may be added later through the same registry.
  • Building the verifier. Test applications and scanners that check a deployed system against the exported crypto specification are a later, separate effort; keyforge's part is to produce the specification and the expectations they will consume.
  • Authenticating callers of the control plane. The control plane takes an authorizer from the host application.

docs.title: Users
docs.text: User Needs Application developer Encrypt and decrypt a value with a purpose and a context; never see key material Operator See key state, rotate or retire a key, know when a key is overdue or not backed up Security reviewer Read the format, the threat model and the audit trail Platform integrator Plug in retention and approval policy before destruction; supply provider and storage

Data keys are unwrapped once and cached in process; a control-plane or provider outage does not stop cached reads NFR2 Fail closed: with no usable key, operations fail rather than weaken NFR3 Rotation is online and resumable; it never requires a maintenance window NFR4 Key material is never logged, returned in errors or written to audit events NFR5 Standard primitives only, with published test vectors and fuzzing of the envelope parser NFR6 Library-first: the library is the product; the CLI and service are thin adapters over it NFR7 Works on a single host with SQLite or with PostgreSQL, without code changes NFR8 Public-ready repository and history from the first commit NFR9 Algorithm choice is a generic selector with fips and standard profiles; the first release runs in the standard profile with AES-256-GCM only, and non-approved algorithms are out of scope. Post-quantum algorithms are adopted from the Go standard library, hybrid first, when they are scoped

docs.title: Success criteria
docs.text:
1. An application can encrypt and decrypt through keyforge using only the local provider, with no configuration beyond a key file path.
  2. A KEK rotation on a store holding a million wrapped keys completes online with no change to application data, and reads during the rotation succeed.
  3. A KEK that has been rotated out can be retired only through the guarded, delayed path, and a guard that refuses leaves the key usable.
  4. Restoring the keyring from a backup that predates a rotation is detected and reported before it can lose data.
  5. An external reviewer can reconstruct, from the format specification alone, how any ciphertext was produced.
  6. (v0.2.0) A disaster-recovery drill runs with no person involved, restores the registry and keyring from backup in an isolated environment, decrypts a sentinel for every retained key version, reports its recovery time and recovery point against configured limits, and produces a report whose conclusions are marked as inferred and whose objective results are marked as verified.

docs.title: Out of scope for v0.1.0
docs.text: Cloud KMS providers, asymmetric KEKs, signing-key management, a remote service mode and certificate lifecycle. The rotation and disaster-recovery drills (FR10b to FR10d) follow in v0.2.0. The interfaces are designed so each fits without changing stored data.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Which managed KMS provider to implement first. The first host's deployment target decides it; it does not block v0.1.0.

Decided in the TRD: the encryption cap per data key (2³⁰), the retirement delay (30 days), where wrapped data keys live (in the registry, in reference mode; beside the data in inline mode), and root-key escrow (the operator's, exercised by the DR drill).
